name: Zinc pyrithione

lead: Zinc pyrithione is the active in many dandruff shampoos. It acts against the yeasts linked to flaking and scalp itch.
It is a standard comparator in dandruff trials. It is not a hair-growth treatment.

paras: It is thought to disrupt fungal membrane transport and raise intracellular copper, damaging iron-sulfur proteins.

US labels warn against use on damaged skin or in young children. The EU classifies it as a reproductive toxicant and has barred it in cosmetics since 2021; it is also toxic to aquatic life as an antifouling agent.

lead: Zinc pyrithione (pyrithione zinc, ZPT) is a zinc coordination complex with antifungal and antibacterial properties. It is the active ingredient in many anti-dandruff shampoos and body washes and is used for seborrheic dermatitis; it is also used in antifouling paints and some textiles.[1][2]

It has been used in dandruff products for decades and is approved as an over-the-counter dandruff ingredient in the US.[2][3] Its regulatory status differs by region: Wikipedia reports that the EU has barred its use in cosmetics since December 2021, citing a reproductive-toxicity classification and environmental concerns.[2]
infobox: OTC dandruff active (US); barred in EU cosmetics since 2021[2]

paras: The main use is relief of dandruff symptoms; a US over-the-counter label states it is for relief of dandruff symptoms and warns against use on wounds or damaged skin or on children under 12 unless directed by a physician.[3] It is also used in paints, coatings and odor-control textiles.[2]

Proposed antifungal mechanisms include disrupting membrane transport and, according to a 2011 yeast study, raising intracellular copper to damage iron-sulfur proteins.[2] Zinc compounds more broadly have a long history in dermatology.[4]

Wikipedia reports that the EU classifies it as a Category 1B reproductive toxicant, that laboratory studies have linked it to DNA damage in skin cells, and that US rules allow up to 2% in rinse-off and 0.25% in leave-on products.[2] A separate review literature documents its toxicity to marine organisms as an antifouling biocide.[5] Wikipedia also cites Swedish and Danish studies indicating it degrades in wastewater treatment and biodegrades quickly, though continuous leaching from boat paint may be toxic to aquatic life.[2]

Zinc pyrithione shampoos have served as the comparator in several dandruff trials, including those against piroctone olamine and ketoconazole shampoos; Wikipedia cites a 1985 study of a zinc pyrithione shampoo and a 2002 trial against ketoconazole in severe dandruff.[2] A review of zinc therapy in dermatology covers zinc pyrithione among topical uses.[4] Antiviral activity has been reported only in cell culture, with no human clinical evidence noted.[2]

timeline.event: EU bars its use in cosmetics.[2]
